To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the arthropod fauna, including herbivore species, was more abundant and diverse on the foliage of mature trees than on that of sapling trees of Pouroumabicolor in a tropical rainforest in Panama.

the abundance of arthropods, including insect herbivores, and species richness of both herbivores and insect species with proven abilities to feed on the host plant are 2–3 times higher on trees than saplings, and that many insect herbivores prefer or are restricted to one or the other host stage.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the abundance and species richness for herbivores were 3–4 times higher in the canopy than on saplings.
the abundance and species richness (but not the diversity) of herbivores on trees were higher than those on saplings.
insect herbivores are less abundant and species-rich on saplings than on conspecific trees, but this is not a general rule for all tropical trees.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the canopy of wet tropical forests is not a uniform habitat, and that the spatial distribution of insect herbivore communities is influenced by the availability of food resources and the structure of the forest.
the abundance and diversity of insect herbivore communities on saplings and mature trees of a common tropical tree species differ substantially.
insect herbivore communities on saplings are not representative of those on mature trees in the upper canopy of tropical wet forests.
